extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, dataset builders, and ML practitioners working on caption-contest/humor generation and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, sampling, deduplicating, and evaluating datasets and models for New Yorker-style caption matching, quality-ranking, and explanation generation tasks. Covers instance construction, annotation, prompt design, automatic metrics, and human evaluation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming matching instances
rubrics_metrics.description: For each high quality caption, create a matching instance that serves as the correct answer; randomly assign captions to mismatched contests to form negative, mismatched sets to serve as false options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constraints on the random assignment: 1) assign within cross-validation splits only, to ensure that training/validation/testing captions are disjoint; and 2) construct the corpus with no answer-only biases by performing the negative assignment such that each answer appears exactly once as a correct answer and exactly 4 times as an incorrect answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming quality-ranking instances
rubrics_metrics.description: For each high quality caption, sample from the larger set of submissions captions that are just “okay” to form quality ranking pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crowd ratings are available (later contests), discard the top third and bottom third by mean crowd rating — the middle tertile forms the “okay” set. For earlier contests without ratings, train a text-only quality ranking model (conditioned on caption text) using crowd-labelled data to estimate quality and sample accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling contests with missing entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some early contests were missing entries, limiting negative sampling to a subset of contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 25 contests from early contest history were missing entries, sampling negatives is limited to 679 contests; account for this when constructing quality-ranking instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduplicate exact-copy captions for 'okay' sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduplicate on string matching so that “okay” captions are not exact copies of the identified high quality captions or any other sampled “okay” captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove exact duplicates before sampling to ensure 'okay' set contains distinct textual instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-ranking model training corpus construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a training corpus for quality ranking by selecting top and bottom entries per contest according to mean crowdsourced score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the top and bottom 1000 entries from each contest (by mean crowdscore) to form a dataset of ~506K captions. Form two sets of labelled data based on contest parity (even vs. odd) and train/validate separate models (T5-Large) on these splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-ranking model evaluation targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the quality-ranking model's ability to identify bad vs. very-good captions using standard precision-at-k metrics and validation accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported average validation accuracy ~65%; higher precision in identifying the 'bad' label: precision-at-10 = 83, precision-at-20 = 77, precision-at-30 = 72. Identifying very good captions is harder: precision-at-10 = 77, precision-at-20 = 73, precision-at-30 = 70.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discarding low-predicted-score entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the trained quality-ranking models to filter contest submissions without crowd ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform inference on all captions in contests without crowd ratings and discard the 25% of entries with the lowest predicted score. Low-scoring entries often lack New Yorker 'gestalt', have many typos/formatting issues, or include submitter contact information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of very low-quality captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed common characteristics of captions that should be discarded as low quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: they don’t have the gestalt of a New Yorker caption, they have many typos/formatting issues, they include the contact information of the submitter, or they are nonsensical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling 'okay' captions (matching constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting an 'okay' caption to pair with a high-quality caption, control for superficial confounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample an 'okay' caption with: 1) similar estimated quality according to the text-only models; 2) similar length in words; 3) similar length in characters; 4) similar amount of punctuation; and 5) a dissimilar SBERT embedding (to avoid near-duplicates/conceptual clones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic deduplication via SBERT + hierarchical clustering
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform semantic deduplication to reduce redundancy after basic filtering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract SentenceBERT embeddings for each entry, compute hierarchical clustering into 0.7 · N clusters, and sample a single representative from each cluster. This removes about 30% of the data with close neighbors in the final set (e.g., many 'tastes like chicken' variants downsampled to one exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation corpus annotation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a corpus of human-written explanations for high-quality captions to train/evaluate explanation models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample a high-quality caption per contest (prefer New Yorker finalists; otherwise high-quality crowd captions). One author annotated explanations for 704 sampled captions, understanding 651 and writing an explanation for each; the resulting corpus has a mean of ~60 words per explanation and total ~39.3K words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt/system behavior for explanation/matching tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: System prompt guidelines for a model acting as an expert CaptionContestGPT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be well versed in New Yorker Caption contest history and humor theories; follow contest weekly; analyze entries and winners; think step-by-step but not overly verbose; express uncertainty in reasoning but ultimately pick a single best answer and respond in the requested format. For multi-choice tasks, reason step-by-step and end with 'Answer: X'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic evaluation metrics for explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard automatic metrics to evaluate generated explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report BLEU-4 (higher is better), ROUGE-L (higher is better), and Perplexity (lower is better). Note: log probabilities (and thus perplexity) are unavailable for some APIs (GPT-3.5/GPT-4), so PPL cannot always be computed. Prefer human evaluations for higher-quality measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reporting and settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Report results averaged over cross-validation splits and compare zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned model variants across settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 5 cross-validation splits for averages; distinguish From Pixels (FP) vs From Description (FD) settings at test time; mark best results per setting; show differences between zero-shot, 5-shot, and fine-tuned variants in figures and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human vs. machine preference evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pairwise human judgments to compare machine-generated explanations/captions with human-authored references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple annotators (e.g., 3) per example and report cases where machine output was preferred by all annotators (e.g., GPT-4 5-shot preferred to human in 8/130 cases by 3/3 annotators). Perform close-reading of these cases to understand why machines were preferred (e.g., more succinct, mention meaningful detail or pop-culture reference missed by humans). Also report cases where machines are incorrectly preferred and analyze errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative analysis of machine strengths and failure modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine where machine-generated explanations/captions outperform or underperform human references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines may be preferred when they are more succinct or mention salient pop-culture details; they can fail by missing subtle points, hallucinating details, or producing non-sequiturs. Use close readings (example-by-example) to diagnose these phenomena.
